title: My tender age
short: The second wing turns from mankind to the speaker's own life, which began in sorrow and sickness.
body: Stanza one narrated the race's history; stanza two repeats the pattern autobiographically. Herbert lost his father in 1596, when he was about three and was troubled by poor health (probably consumption) through much of his life, dying at 39 in 1633; Walton's Life records his ill health. The line also has a general scriptural sense: man is 'born unto trouble' (Job 5:7) and conceived in sin (Psalm 51:5), so personal suffering mirrors inherited guilt.

sources.cite: F. E. Hutchinson (ed.), The Works of George Herbert (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1941), commentary on this poem
Izaak Walton, The Life of Mr. George Herbert (1670)

title: sicknesses and shame
short: Bodily illness and moral disgrace are both read as God's correction of sin, a standard providential reading of suffering.
body: Herbert frequently treats illness as divine discipline: the 'Affliction' poems in The Temple explore it at length. The idea is biblical, 'whom the Lord loveth he chasteneth' (Hebrews 12:6). The pairing of sickness and shame joins body and conscience; the line is answered at the stanza's end by the transformed word 'Affliction', which now 'advances' rather than punishes. The rhyme 'sinne' / 'thinne' links moral cause and bodily effect in the narrowing wing.

sources.cite: Helen Wilcox (ed.), The English Poems of George Herbert (Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 2007), notes to this poem

title: Most thinne
short: The narrowest line of the second wing, parallel to 'Most poore': the speaker is wasted in body and in spirit.
body: 'Thinne' is literal (emaciated by sickness) and figurative (spiritually depleted), and it describes the line itself, which is as thin as the printed wing can be. The exact parallel with 'Most poore' in the first stanza shows that the individual life recapitulates the Fall. Summers notes that the shape is not decoration: the reader sees the diminution before reading it.

sources.cite: Joseph H. Summers, George Herbert: His Religion and Art (London: Chatto & Windus, 1954), ch. 'The Poem as Hieroglyph'
F. E. Hutchinson (ed.), The Works of George Herbert (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1941), commentary on this poem

title: combine
short: To be joined or united with Christ; the speaker asks for union, not merely help.
body: 'Combine' here means to unite closely, a sense already current in Herbert's day. It corresponds to 'O let me rise' in stanza one but is more intimate: rising follows from union. The doctrine is the Pauline union with Christ in death and resurrection (Romans 6:5; Galatians 2:20, 'I live; yet not I, but Christ liveth in me').

title: imp
short: Falconry term: to graft new feathers onto a bird's damaged wing so that it can fly again.
body: To 'imp' was to splice feathers into a hawk's broken or moulted wing to restore its flight; the word comes from Old English impian, to graft (originally of plants). Herbert's conceit makes Christ's wing the source of the new feathers: the speaker's broken wing flies because it is joined to Christ's. The technical term would be familiar to readers of the hawking manuals and of Shakespeare ('Imp out our drooping country's broken wing', Richard II, Act 2, scene 1). It completes the poem's turn from the visual shape of wings to their use.

sources.cite: F. E. Hutchinson (ed.), The Works of George Herbert (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1941), commentary on this poem
Helen Wilcox (ed.), The English Poems of George Herbert (Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 2007), notes to this poem

title: Affliction shall advance
short: The personal counterpart of the fortunate fall: suffering, joined to Christ, becomes the means of the soul's ascent.
body: The last line answers the last line of stanza one ('Then shall the fall further the flight in me'): 'Affliction' takes the place of 'the fall', and 'advance' of 'further'. What punished in line 3 now propels. Herbert uses 'affliction' with weight throughout The Temple, where five poems bear the title. The thought is Pauline: 'our light affliction ... worketh for us a far more exceeding and eternal weight of glory' (2 Corinthians 4:17).

sources.cite: Helen Wilcox (ed.), The English Poems of George Herbert (Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 2007), notes to this poem
Richard Strier, Love Known: Theology and Experience in George Herbert's Poetry (Chicago: University of Chicago Press, 1983)

title: victorie
short: The singular of stanza one's 'victories': Christ's Easter triumph now felt within the speaker.
body: As in stanza one, the source is 1 Corinthians 15:57: 'thanks be to God, which giveth us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ'. Here the speaker asks to 'feel' that victory, moving from celebration (sing) to experience (feel). The shift from plural to singular narrows the cosmic triumph to one life, as the whole second stanza narrows history to autobiography.

sources.cite: Helen Wilcox (ed.), The English Poems of George Herbert (Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 2007), notes to this poem
